title: May we hear what is good
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hookLine: six seekers wait a year to ask, and the chant begins with the ears
carry: shruti: the sacred begins with hearing
tomorrow: why would a student ask Brahman not to turn away?

lines: THE CHANT BEGINS AT THE EARS.
cards: Six seekers walk up to the sage Pippalada, each carrying firewood, the old sign of a student asking to be taught. Each has a question: where do living beings come from? What holds up the body?
What is Om? In the Prashna Upanishad, Pippalada doesn't answer. Live here one more year, he says, with discipline, simplicity and trust.
Then ask, and if I know, I'll tell you everything. A whole year, just to be ready to listen. And the chant that opens that Upanishad begins with the ears.

teach.b: The chant is known by its first words, bhadram karnebhih, and tradition sets it with the Prashna, the Mundaka and the Mandukya. Its lines come from a hymn of the Rig Veda.
In plain words: O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good. May we see with our eyes what is good. With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span the gods have set.
Then: Om, peace, peace, peace. Bhadram means good, auspicious, what does a person well. Notice where it starts.
Not with the self, not with the big questions. With the ears. That's no accident in Hinduism.
The Vedas are called shruti, which means what is heard.
For centuries they lived in voices, teacher to student, ear to ear.
And in the Brihadaranyaka, Yajnavalkya tells his wife Maitreyi that the self is to be heard about, reflected on, and meditated on; teachers of Vedanta read those as three steps, with hearing first.
If hearing comes first, what comes in through the ears matters.

teach.h: MAY WE HEAR WHAT IS GOOD.
teach.b: That's why the six seekers waited a year, and why the whole room asks, together, before a word of the text: may what we hear be good.

how: Bhadram karnebhih is chanted as the peace chant of the Mundaka, Prashna and Mandukya Upanishads, before and after their study, and is also used to open prayers and gatherings. Many Hindu homes play chants or bhajans in the morning, simply to be heard.

games.q: your cousin asks why the Vedas were learned by ear for centuries instead of just read. what fits?
o: they're shruti, 'what is heard': hearing from a teacher is how they're received.
nobody could write back then, so it was the only way.
they were short, so writing them down wasn't worth it.
games.why: shruti means what is heard. the tradition puts hearing first: hear, then reflect, then meditate.

practice: Many Hindu homes start the day with a chant or a bhajan playing, simply to be heard. If you have one, play it softly now and only listen.
If not, let the room's sounds arrive on their own, near and far, and notice each came in through the ears. Near the end, choose one sound that does you good and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: The peace chants, and today bhadram karnebhih: may we hear with our ears what is good. Shruti, what is heard, starts there.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the good, with the ears; the first words of the peace chant.

carryVoice: To carry: shruti, the sacred begins with hearing. So ask to hear what is good. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.89.8 (bhadram karnebhih shrinuyama devah…) and 1.89.6 (svasti na indro…), chanted as the peace chant of the Mundaka, Prashna and Mandukya Upanishads
Prashna Upanishad 1.1–2 (six seekers come to Pippalada with fuel in hand; he asks them to stay a year with tapas, brahmacharya and shraddha, then ask)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on, meditated on), read in Vedanta as shravana, manana, nididhyasana
